findings.summary: Alloys are metallic mixtures of two or more elements designed to improve properties like strength, hardness, or corrosion resistance. Most commercial metals are alloyed rather than used in pure form. The base metal typically dissolves other elements in a molten state, forming either a single-phase solid solution or a multi-phase microstructure. Mechanical behavior changes significantly; for example, adding carbon to iron creates steel with greater strength than pure iron, while chromium enhances corrosion resistance. Alloys are classified as substitutional or interstitial based on atomic arrangement, and may be homogeneous or heterogeneous. Common examples include steel, brass, bronze, and specialized aerospace alloys.

mechanisms.title: Solid solution strengthening
mechanisms.explanation: When alloying elements dissolve into the base metal's crystal lattice, they distort the lattice and impede dislocation movement, increasing hardness and strength. This occurs whether the alloy forms a single-phase solid solution or a multi-phase microstructure.

mechanisms.title: Phase transformation and microstructure control
mechanisms.explanation: Cooling rate and element solubility determine whether an alloy forms a homogeneous single phase or separates into multiple phases. Slow cooling promotes homogeneous structures, while rapid cooling can trap supersaturated elements that later precipitate to reinforce the crystal lattice internally.
